title: System development life cycle and project planning
overview: A system project changes people, processes, technology, and responsibilities—not technology alone. This week connects project planning with the four-stage sequence Plan → Analyze → Design → Implement, introduces terms and tools used to make project decisions visible, and considers how early user involvement and HIM responsibilities support fit, trustworthy information, and adoption.
objectives: Explain that a system project is a change to people, processes, technology, and responsibilities.
Explain how planning makes the problem, scope, budget, risks, and success measures explicit.
Explain how early user involvement improves fit and creates buy-in.

sections.body: A system project is a change to people, processes, technology, and responsibilities. This definition matters because a technically configured system is only one part of the change: people use it, workflows accommodate it, and responsibilities shape how information is handled. Planning therefore makes the problem, scope, budget, risks, and success measures explicit. Scope identifies the work included, excluded, and prioritized; feasibility asks whether the organization can afford, support, and sustain the option. Stakeholders are the people who use, own, support, and are affected by the system. Change management concerns how people adopt the new way of working. These terms help a project team describe not only what it intends to configure, but also what work and adoption the project entails.
sections.title: A project changes work, not just technology

sections.body: The framework proceeds through Plan → Analyze → Design → Implement. In Plan, the team sets goals, scope, budget, team, and measures. In Analyze, it collects and evaluates information about the current state. In Design, it specifies workflows, data, interfaces, and controls. In Implement, it configures and tests the system, trains users, goes live, and improves the system. The stages organize the work and make it possible to ask what happens, who is responsible, and where control is needed. In the hospital document-management example, the team defines the problem and studies the current workflow before setting scope, evaluating feasibility, designing, testing, training users, and improving the system after implementation.
sections.title: Organize the work through four stages

sections.body: The planning tools serve different purposes. A Gantt chart makes task start and finish times and dependencies visible. A PERT chart focuses on activity sequence and uncertainty. A project plan describes activities, owners, resources, and milestones. A feasibility study examines whether the project is practical and sustainable. These tools are not interchangeable: a timeline and task dependencies are different from a view of activity sequence and uncertainty, while a description of project assignments and resources differs from an assessment of whether the option can be sustained. In the document-management project, the team can choose a tool according to whether it needs to organize tasks, clarify ownership and resources, consider activity uncertainty, or assess feasibility.
sections.title: Select planning tools by the question they answer

sections.body: Early user involvement improves fit and creates buy-in. Fit concerns whether the system supports its intended users, work, outputs, and decisions; user participation provides an opportunity to consider those needs while the project is being planned and designed. Adoption is also part of the project: change management addresses how people adopt the new way of working, and implementation includes testing, training, going live, and improvement. HIM responsibilities keep information work in view. HIM professionals explain system purpose by identifying users, inputs, outputs, decisions, and limits; protect meaning through definitions, standards, terminology, mapping, and consistent interpretation; check identity, completeness, accuracy, validity, timeliness, and consistency; support privacy, security, appropriate access, auditability, and responsible disclosure; and improve workflow through feedback, testing, training, monitoring, and root-cause correction.
